ca_anthony_s_boulder.blurb: Anthony's Boulder is one of the five boulders that form the middle of Central Atlantis, part of the Tramway bouldering zone in the San Jacinto Mountains. It has nine problems, all graded in the V scale. Most sit in the easy range from VB to V1, then the grades jump to a handful of hard lines between V4 and V7, so it suits both warm-up laps and projecting. The surrounding trees keep the boulder in shade through the whole day, which is unusual here and makes it a useful option when other blocks in the zone are baking.

ca_parcher_s_bluff.blurb: Parcher's Bluff is a small granite cliff in the South Lake corridor above Bishop, high in the Eastern Sierra. Aspens and wildflowers grow around its base, and the face looks to the southwest, so mornings stay cool while the rock warms later in the day. Nine routes cover trad, sport and one top-rope line, running from 5.6 up to 5.11, with most clustered around 5.10. Climbs are short, roughly 40 to 60 feet, and bolts back up the spots where natural gear is thin. Late summer and fall are the comfortable seasons for visiting.

ca_bronto_rock.blurb: Bronto Rock is a cluster of small monzogranite formations, each with its own top, sitting north of Stirrup Rock in the Stirrup Tank section of Joshua Tree National Park's Pinto Basin. It holds nine routes, mainly traditional lines with a couple of top-rope problems and a single bolted climb. Grades start at 5.4 and reach 5.11, with a spread of moderate cracks and a few harder pitches, making it a handy stop for a mixed party. Stirrup Tank is on the park's eastern side, away from the busier western zones.

ca_brit_corridor.blurb: Brit Corridor is a narrow gap cutting through the Screamer Rocks formation, in the Split Rocks West zone of Joshua Tree National Park's Pinto Basin. The passage trends northwest to southeast, and its monzogranite walls hold nine routes, six of them traditional and three bolted. Most of the climbing sits at 5.10, with one climb in the 5.11 range and a few easier options near 5.4 to 5.8, including some two-pitch lines. The walk from the parking lot is short, and the walls of the corridor give a compact, enclosed setting for a few hours of climbing.

ca_cap_rock_south_face.blurb: This broad, slabby face rises straight out of the main Cap Rock parking area in Joshua Tree National Park, so the walk to the base is close to nothing. Picnic tables and an outhouse sit nearby. All nine routes are traditional, on monzogranite, running from 5.8 to 5.13, with the bulk between 5.9 and 5.10 and one hard test-piece at the top end. Cracks and faces break up the slabs, and the setting works best in cooler weather. The short approach and moderate grades make it a straightforward place to start a trad day.

ca_chimney_rock_north_face.blurb: This face belongs to Chimney Rock, a large jumbled formation near Lucerne Valley in California's High Desert, on quartz monzonite. It has nine routes, seven of them bolted and two traditional. The grades lean easy: several climbs fall between 5.6 and 5.9, with a single 5.11 as the hardest. Most of the lines are low-effort slabs, and a few cracks add variety. Reaching the base means walking around either end of the formation and then heading uphill, which takes a short while from the parking area, so it works well for beginners and anyone building up on easy sport.

ca_chuckwalla_wall.blurb: Chuckwalla Wall is the main wall of the North Gorge in the Owens River Gorge, near Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, at roughly 6,000 feet. Nine routes, eight bolted and one traditional, run from 5.10 to 5.12, with the greater part at 5.11. The climbing is slabby and technical, a good match for climbers who like precise footwork over brute strength. The wall was cleaned and re-equipped in 2024, so the lines are in fresh condition. The gorge itself is known for sport climbing and can be climbed through much of the year, although midsummer gets hot.
